artifacts.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
artifacts.author: Hospital Medicine Service
artifacts.body: 29-year-old female presented with 2-month history of polyuria, polydipsia, blurred vision, and unintentional weight loss (8 lb over 3 months). Found to have severe hyperglycemia on admission. Diagnosed with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus. Treated with IV fluids and insulin per hyperglycemia protocol; transitioned to subcutaneous insulin glargine 10 units at bedtime plus metformin 500 mg BID at discharge. Education provided on diabetes self-management, though patient reported feeling overwhelmed during teaching session. Referred to outpatient nutrition counseling and diabetes education within 2 weeks of discharge. No evidence of diabetic ketoacidosis on admission labs. Follow-up with PCP and endocrinology arranged.

objectives.text: Develop an appropriate PES (Problem, Etiology, Signs/Symptoms) statement reflecting medication non-adherence, high refined carbohydrate intake, and irregular meal timing in the context of newly diagnosed T2DM.
Apply motivational interviewing techniques to explore the patient's ambivalence about lifestyle change, affirming her strengths while eliciting her own motivation for behavior change.
Identify and address lifestyle and behavioral barriers to nutrition therapy, including work schedule constraints, cultural food traditions, and family meal preparation dynamics.
Integrate medication management considerations (metformin timing with meals, insulin glargine and hypoglycemia risk) into nutrition counseling and meal timing recommendations.
Elicit sensitive psychosocial information (guilt, embarrassment, fear of restrictive diets, undisclosed supplement research) using rapport-building and non-judgmental, open-ended questioning.

She is married; her husband works long hours too, and her mother-in-law lives nearby and often cooks traditional meals for the family. She enjoys solving complex problems at work and tends to approach her health the same analytical way, which sometimes backfires when the body doesn't behave like a system she can debug.

scenario.studentBrief: You are the dietetics student conducting a telehealth nutrition assessment visit with Nisha Patel, a 29-year-old woman recently discharged from her first hospitalization for uncontrolled Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus. She has been referred for outpatient medical nutrition therapy. Review her chart before the visit; your goals are to complete a nutrition assessment, identify a nutrition diagnosis, and begin patient-centered counseling.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Follow-up nutrition counseling visit after first hospitalization for uncontrolled Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
scenario.openingLine: Hi... thank you for seeing me. I've been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and was just hospitalized for the first time, and honestly I'm still trying to wrap my head around all of it.
tasks: Complete a comprehensive nutrition assessment including diet history, anthropometrics, relevant labs, and medication-related barriers
Identify at least one appropriate nutrition diagnosis (PES statement) based on assessment findings
Use motivational interviewing techniques to explore the patient's readiness for change and address her ambivalence
Identify cultural, occupational, and psychosocial barriers to nutrition therapy and collaboratively generate at least one realistic, patient-centered goal
Document the encounter using the ADIME format

profile.setting: Telehealth video visit; patient at home in her home office, recently discharged from hospital, following up with dietetics for outpatient nutrition counseling
profile.summary: A 29-year-old Indian-American software engineer presents for her first outpatient nutrition counseling visit after a hospitalization for uncontrolled Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus with HbA1c 8.8%. The case teaches nutrition assessment, PES statement formulation, motivational interviewing with an anxious high-health-literacy-seeking-but-overwhelmed patient, and culturally sensitive, barrier-focused counseling around medication adherence and irregular eating patterns.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Excessive carbohydrate intake and irregular meal pattern related to work schedule demands and lack of nutrition-related knowledge, as evidenced by HbA1c 8.8%, fasting glucose 185 mg/dL, skipped breakfasts, large late dinners, and frequent refined carbohydrate/sugary beverage intake.
differential: Food- and nutrition-related knowledge deficit regarding carbohydrate-medication timing
Inconsistent medication adherence related to fear of hypoglycemia and complexity of regimen
Undesirable food choices (high refined carbohydrate/added sugar intake) related to psychological stress and cultural food availability
Altered nutrition-related laboratory values (elevated HbA1c, fasting glucose, dyslipidemia) related to uncontrolled T2DM
keyFindings: BMI 26.1 kg/m2 (overweight), recent unintentional 8 lb weight loss over 3 months prior to diagnosis
Skips breakfast; large lunch; late dinner after 8-9pm; frequent coffee with sugar; evening sugary snacking under stress
Inconsistent metformin and insulin glargine adherence due to work schedule and fear of hypoglycemia
High anxiety, guilt around sugar intake, belief that diabetes reflects personal willpower failure
Fear that nutrition therapy will mean complete elimination of culturally important foods (rice, roti)
Strong family support (husband) but limited control over dinner content due to mother-in-law's traditional cooking
Hidden barrier: has attempted self-directed carb counting but found it unsustainable; has not disclosed independent supplement research
plan: Establish rapport and normalize her anxiety and guilt using reflective listening before introducing education
Provide brief, lay-language explanation of glucose/insulin physiology tailored to her analytical style, checking understanding frequently
Collaboratively identify one or two small, specific behavior changes (e.g., adding a small protein/fiber-containing breakfast, moving largest meal earlier) rather than prescribing elimination diets
Discuss carbohydrate-consistent eating approach aligned with culturally familiar foods (portion-based rice/chapati guidance, not elimination)
Clarify metformin timing with meals to reduce GI side effects and link insulin glargine timing/dose with evening meal pattern to reduce hypoglycemia fear
Address evening/stress-related snacking with alternative coping strategies and collaborative problem-solving
Explore and validate cultural food traditions and festival pressures; identify small modifications rather than avoidance
Screen anxiety symptoms and consider referral to behavioral health if symptoms persist or worsen
Ask directly and non-judgmentally about use of online research/supplements to open disclosure and provide guidance on safety/efficacy
Document assessment and plan using ADIME format; schedule follow-up visit in 2-4 weeks to reassess adherence and readiness for change
Coordinate with endocrinology regarding insulin titration and medication adherence barriers
redFlags: Severe/worsening hyperglycemia symptoms (recurrent polyuria/polydipsia, confusion) warranting urgent re-evaluation
Signs or reported episodes of hypoglycemia (shakiness, diaphoresis, altered mental status) requiring immediate medication adjustment review
Significant unintentional weight loss continuing despite treatment, which could suggest inadequate glycemic control or other pathology
Escalating anxiety symptoms (panic attacks, inability to function) warranting behavioral health referral
Use of unverified supplements that could interact with metformin or insulin
educationPoints: Diabetes is a chronic metabolic condition influenced by genetics, physiology, and environment — not simply a result of personal willpower
Carbohydrate-consistent eating (balanced portions and timing) is generally more sustainable and effective than complete elimination diets
Traditional foods like rice and roti can remain part of her diet through portion awareness and pairing with protein/fiber, not elimination
Regular meal timing, including not skipping breakfast, helps stabilize blood glucose and may reduce evening overeating
Taking metformin with meals as prescribed reduces GI side effects; consistent meal timing supports more predictable insulin glargine action and reduces hypoglycemia risk
Mild anxiety and guilt around food choices are common after a new diabetes diagnosis and do not reflect personal failure
Open communication about outside research (supplements, online information) with her care team helps ensure safety and avoid interactions
Small, specific, achievable behavior changes are more sustainable than large overhauls, especially given her demanding work schedule
